notes.body:
The honest answer is that وَلَهَ and وَلِهَ come from a **different root** than الهٔ. The root of وَلَهَ is و-ل-ه, while the root of الهٔ is أ-ل-ه — two separate entries in the classical Arabic lexicon, not parent and child. A traditional dictionary lists them under different headings, and a morphologist would not derive one from the other.

What the chapter is actually doing is building a **semantic portrait** — gathering words from neighboring roots that circle the same human experience: the aching devotion, the desperate turning-toward, the loss of self in a beloved. A concept as vast as what الهٔ names has echoes scattered across roots that touch the same emotional terrain, and the chapter arranges them like facets of a single gem.

In Arabic scholarship, what the chapter calls a composite word is closer to what linguists call a **semantic field** — a cluster of roots that illuminate one another because they orbit the same reality. None of these words is invented; each is attested in classical Arabic with the meaning the chapter assigns it. The insight is not in claiming they share a root; it is in placing them side by side so that together they map a territory no single root could cover.

One final nuance: in Semitic linguistics, the first radical of a root can sometimes alternate between a glottal (أ) and a semi-vowel (و) across related ancient languages, hinting at a distant **shared ancestry**. But that is the archaeology of Proto-Semitic, not a claim the chapter makes — and it does not change the practical Arabic reality that أ-ل-ه and و-ل-ه are two distinct roots.

notes.quote: Another derivative of the word الہ comes from وَلِہَ which means to become astounded
etymology: وَلَهَ (frantic love): from the root و-ل-ه, meaning to be distracted and distraught — as a mother undone by the loss of her child. The root captures the state where the mind loses its grip before overwhelming love or grief. It yields مُوَلَّه, the one driven to distraction by the absence of a beloved.

أَلَهَ (to worship): from the root أ-ل-ه, the base of الهٔ itself, carrying the senses of seeking refuge, being bewildered, and surrendering completely. It is what a baby does turning to its mother for milk — and what a soul does when it finally meets the one who holds it entirely.

notes.body:
The heart is not a blank container — its shape is worn into it by longing itself. Every الہ we construct, every career we prostrate ourselves to and every beloved we lose our minds over, is the heart pressing something against its own contours and calling it a fit. When those things are torn away, the contour does not disappear. **What remains is the shape of the longing itself.**

The meanings of the word الہ — the one you worship, lean on, turn to in desperation, obsess over, are astonished by — are not a random list. They are the architecture of the human heart. Self-created idols do not invent these capacities; **they merely hijack them,** pouring themselves into a mould they did not make.

This is what makes لَا اِلَہَ اِلَّا اللَّہُ so precise. The لَا is not just grammar. It is a deliberate act of clearing — removing the career, the beloved, the numbing habit, the mirror held endlessly up to our own self (نفس). Each removal does not deepen the emptiness; it sharpens the outline. And when every pretender is gone, the اِلَّا points to the only being who satisfies every definition of الہ **without failing even one** — who can be loved with the full force of the heart's capacity and will not diminish, who can be leaned on completely and will not buckle, who can be turned to in desperation and will always receive.

The story of Prophet أیوب makes this luminous. At the height of his suffering, he found that Allah was speaking to him every single day. When his illness was cured and the conversation grew quieter, he grieved. He had discovered the one الہ whose presence is more sustaining than health itself. The idol of comfort had been replaced by **the source of all comfort**.

Ismaili teaching distinguishes between divinity (الهية) and creation as two fundamental modes of existence. Everything we ever idolised belongs to creation. Only Allah is الهية itself — not a being who happens to deserve worship, but the very ground from which the concept of الہ draws its meaning. Negating the created does not leave absence. It reveals **what was always there before the idols were built.**

notes.quote: By the negation and the destruction of these self created idols, emerges the understanding of Allah
etymology: الهية: from root أ-ل-ه. الهية is the abstract noun for divinity — the quality of being what the heart was always built to turn toward. The root already carries the meanings of worship, desperate longing, and passionate love; الهية concentrates all of them into a single ontological category. Only Allah possesses it in its absolute, uncreated form.

هوى: from root ه-و-ي, meaning to fall or plunge downward. هوى is the gravitational pull of desire — the heart's descent toward what it craves. The root tells the whole story: desire is a falling, and whatever the heart falls toward becomes, by definition, its الہ.

نفس: from root ن-ف-س, meaning to breathe. نفس is both breath and self — the living, moving interior of a person. The connection to breath is exact: the نفس is never still, always either expanding toward Allah or turning inward to feed its own hungers.

توحید: from root و-ح-د, meaning to be alone, singular, one. توحيد is not merely a belief in oneness but the act of making one — unifying the heart's allegiances until only Allah remains at the centre. The root holds both the statement and the practice inside a single word.
